text: sas_script() writes translation program R script runs library(sasonr). tidy = TRUE, vectorised DATA step becomes dplyr pipe R data frames (script loads dplyr tidylog, every step reports ); steps need sasonr’s runtime run short session block. Without tidy, every SAS step becomes one call step verb session: sas_data_step() holds generated code DATA step SAS text came , sas_proc_sort() sas_proc_means() show options program gave, steps keep SAS text. script gives WORK data sets log sas_run(). sas_script() also takes result sas_run(): script trace run, including steps macro code generated.
code: code2 <- " data lab;   input usubjid $ visit aval;   datalines; S01 1 10 S01 2 12 S02 1 20 S02 2 18 ; run;  data chg;   set lab;   by usubjid;   retain base;   if first.usubjid then base = aval;   chg = aval - base; run; " sas_script(sas_translate(code2), tidy = TRUE) #> # Translation of the SAS program, written by sasonr. #> # Tidy form: steps that need a sasonr session run in a session block. #> library(sasonr) #> library(dplyr) #> library(tidylog) #>  #> # data lab;  (SAS line 2) #> # ---- DATA LAB (SAS line 2) -- level L1 #> # L1: no cross-row state #> lab <- sas_read_input(sas_infile_open(c("S01 1 10", "S01 2 12", "S02 1 20", "S02 2 18"), c(5L, 6L, 7L, 8L), opts = list(lines = 1L, end_text = ";")), list(items = list( #>     list(k = "var", name = "usubjid", disp = "usubjid", char = TRUE, len = 8L, mode = "list"), #>     list(k = "var", name = "visit", disp = "visit", char = FALSE, len = NA_integer_, mode = "list"), #>     list(k = "var", name = "aval", disp = "aval", char = FALSE, len = NA_integer_, mode = "list") #>   ), hold = "")) |> #>   select(usubjid, visit, aval) #>  #> # data chg;  (SAS line 12) #> # ---- DATA CHG (SAS line 12) -- level L2 #> # L2: BY-group processing (FIRST./LAST.); retained value carried forward (baseline / LOCF) #> chg <- lab |> #>   sas_check_sorted("usubjid", FALSE) |> #>   mutate( #>     first.usubjid = sas_first(usubjid) #>   ) |> #>   group_by(.grp = cumsum(first.usubjid)) |> #>   mutate( #>     base = as.numeric(dplyr::first(aval)) #>   ) |> #>   ungroup() |> #>   mutate( #>     chg = sas_arith(aval, base, "-") #>   ) |> #>   select(usubjid, visit, aval, base, chg) code3 <- " data adsl;   input usubjid $ age;   datalines; S01 70 S02 41 ; run; proc sort data=adsl out=bysubj; by descending age; run; " sas_script(sas_translate(code3)) #> # Translation of the SAS program, written by sasonr. #> library(sasonr) #>  #> s <- sas_session() #>  #> s |> sas_data_step("adsl", \(work) { #>   # ---- DATA ADSL (SAS line 2) -- level L1 #>   # L1: no cross-row state #>   .d <- sas_read_input(sas_infile_open(c("S01 70", "S02 41"), c(5L, 6L), opts = list(lines = 1L, end_text = ";")), list(items = list( #>       list(k = "var", name = "usubjid", disp = "usubjid", char = TRUE, len = 8L, mode = "list"), #>       list(k = "var", name = "age", disp = "age", char = FALSE, len = NA_integer_, mode = "list") #>     ), hold = "")) #>   work$adsl <- .d |> #>     dplyr::select(usubjid, age) #> }, sas = r"(data adsl; #>   input usubjid $ age; #>   datalines; #> S01 70 #> S02 41 #> ;)", line = 2L) #>  #> s |> sas_proc_sort("data=adsl out=bysubj", by = "descending age", line = 9L)

what: Independent Implementation of SAS 9.4 Program Semantics in R
title: Independent Implementation of SAS 9.4 Program Semantics in R
text: Execute SAS programs R engine. sasonr independent implementation SAS 9.4 program semantics R, written reference publicly available SAS 9.4 documentation. Features support fail loud instead approximated. Compatibility SAS guaranteed. sasonr affiliated , endorsed , sponsored SAS Institute Inc. SAS registered trademark SAS Institute Inc. sasonr parses SAS source code (DATA step, macro language, PROC SQL growing set procedures) abstract syntax tree hand-written lexer, recursive-descent parser Pratt expression parser, executes R: DATA steps compiled tidyverse code, PROC SQL runs DuckDB. Three ways use : SAS programs R - execute SAS programs R session. Deterministic SAS R migration - sas_translate() produces R code without language model. R / SAS double programming - one programmer writes R, writes SAS code runs sasonr platform. Design rules: Deterministic: language model involved run time. Fail loud: language feature sasonr support raises sasonr_unsupported condition SAS line number instead guessing. Status: early development, CRAN.

code: # ABS: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # The absolute value of a negative number drops the sign. sas_f_abs(-3.5)  # abs(-3.5) = 3.5 #> [1] 3.5  # The absolute value of zero is zero. sas_f_abs(0)  # abs(0) = 0 #> [1] 0  # A missing argument (.) gives a missing result. sas_f_abs(NA_real_)  # abs(.) = . #> [1] NA  # A special missing value such as .A also gives the ordinary missing value (.). sas_f_abs(sas_missing(".A"))  # abs(.A) = . #> [1] NA

title: SAS ANYALNUM(string <, start>) — sas_f_anyalnum
code: # ANYALNUM: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # The search starts at position 1; the first letter or digit is 'a' at position # 3, after two blanks. sas_f_anyalnum("  ab1")  # anyalnum('  ab1') = 3 #> [1] 3  # No letter or digit occurs in the string, so the result is 0. sas_f_anyalnum("!!!")  # anyalnum('!!!') = 0 #> [1] 0  # Negative start -3 searches leftwards from position 3: the first alphanumeric # character found is '1' at position 2. sas_f_anyalnum("a1!", -3)  # anyalnum('a1!', -3) = 2 #> [1] 2  # Start 3 searches rightwards from position 3, which holds only '!', so nothing # is found and the result is 0. sas_f_anyalnum("!a!", 3)  # anyalnum('!a!', 3) = 0 #> [1] 0

SAS code informat name , string. qq Error-control modifier written informat: ” (default) writes note sets error flag invalid data; '?' suppresses note; '??' suppresses note error flag. .Internal: source position c(line, column) used log NOTEs.

title: SAS INPUT(source, <? | ??> informat.) — sas_f_input
code: # INPUT: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # INPUT reads the character value '123' with the numeric informat 8. and # returns the number 123. sas_f_input("123", list(name = "", w = 8L, d = NA_integer_, char = FALSE, text = "8."))  # input('123', 8.) = 123 #> [1] 123  # With informat 4.2 and no decimal point in the data, the last 2 digits are # taken as decimals: 12.34. sas_f_input("1234", list(name = "", w = 4L, d = 2L, char = FALSE, text = "4.2"))  # input('1234', 4.2) = 12.34 #> [1] 12.34  # The COMMA informat removes the commas before reading the number. sas_f_input("1,234", list(name = "comma", w = 8L, d = NA_integer_, char = FALSE, text = "comma8."))  # input('1,234', comma8.) = 1234 #> [1] 1234  # The ?? modifier suppresses the invalid-data note and the error flag; the # unreadable value gives missing. sas_f_input("abc", list(name = "", w = 8L, d = NA_integer_, char = FALSE, text = "8."), qq = "??")  # input('abc', ?? 8.) = . #> [1] NA  # The character informat $3. reads only the first 3 characters. sas_f_input("abcdef", list(name = "", w = 3L, d = NA_integer_, char = TRUE, text = "$3."))  # input('abcdef', $3.) = "abc" #> [1] "abc"

code: # INTNX: each call is explained above it and followed by its result # (dates are SAS day counts from 1960-01-01)  # Advance 1 month: the beginning of the next month (alignment 'b' is the # default). sas_f_intnx("month", 21929, 1)  # intnx('month','15JAN2020'd,1) = 21946 #> [1] 21946  # Alignment 'e': the end of the next month. sas_f_intnx("month", 21929, 1, "e")  # intnx('month','15JAN2020'd,1,'e') = 21974 #> [1] 21974  # Alignment 's': the same day in the next month. sas_f_intnx("month", 21929, 1, "s")  # intnx('month','15JAN2020'd,1,'s') = 21960 #> [1] 21960  # Alignment 's' from 31 Jan: the same day does not exist in February, so the # last day (29 Feb 2020). sas_f_intnx("month", 21945, 1, "s")  # intnx('month','31JAN2020'd,1,'s') = 21974 #> [1] 21974  # A negative increment goes back: the beginning of the previous month. sas_f_intnx("month", 21929, -1)  # intnx('month','15JAN2020'd,-1) = 21884 #> [1] 21884

SAS code format name , string. align Optional alignment written format: 'l' left-aligns (-L), 'r' right-aligns (-R), 'c' centers (-C) formatted value within width. Default none.

title: SAS PUT(source, format.) — sas_f_put
code: # PUT: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # PUT formats 3.14159 with the w.d format 8.3: rounded to 3 decimals, # right-aligned in 8 columns. sas_f_put(3.14159, list(name = "", w = 8L, d = 3L, char = FALSE, text = "8.3"))  # put(3.14159, 8.3) = "   3.142" #> [1] "   3.142"  # The Z5. format pads the number with leading zeros to width 5. sas_f_put(42, list(name = "z", w = 5L, d = NA_integer_, char = FALSE, text = "z5."))  # put(42, z5.) = "00042" #> [1] "00042"  # The COMMA10. format inserts thousands separators, right-aligned in 10 # columns. sas_f_put(1234567, list(name = "comma", w = 10L, d = NA_integer_, char = FALSE, text = "comma10."))  # put(1234567, comma10.) = " 1,234,567" #> [1] " 1,234,567"  # A missing value is written as a period; for a w.d format it sits where the # decimal point would be. sas_f_put(NA_real_, list(name = "", w = 8L, d = 2L, char = FALSE, text = "8.2"))  # put(., 8.2) = "     ." #> [1] "     .  "  # The character format $5. writes 'ab' in a 5-character field, padded with # trailing blanks. sas_f_put("ab", list(name = "", w = 5L, d = NA_integer_, char = TRUE, text = "$5."))  # put('ab', $5.) = "ab" #> [1] "ab   "

title: SAS PUTC(source, format <, w>) — sas_f_putc
code: # PUTC: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # PUTC applies a character format given as a string; $5. pads 'abc' to width 5. sas_f_putc("abc", "$5.")  # putc('abc', '$5.') = "abc" #> [1] "abc  "  # The $UPCASE3. format writes the value in upper case. sas_f_putc("abc", "$upcase3.")  # putc('abc', '$upcase3.') = "ABC" #> [1] "ABC"  # $HEX6. writes 616263 (two hex digits per character); a new variable gets the # length of the first argument (3), so SAS stores 616. substr(sas_f_putc("abc", "$hex6."), 1, 3)  # putc('abc', '$hex6.') = "616" #> [1] "616"  # The format $3. writes only the first 3 characters. sas_f_putc("abcdef", "$3.")  # putc('abcdef', '$3.') = "abc" #> [1] "abc"

title: SAS PUTN(source, format <, w <, d>>) — sas_f_putn
code: # PUT: each call is explained above it and followed by its result # (dates are SAS day counts from 1960-01-01)  # Write 123 with the 8. format: right-aligned in 8 columns. sas_f_putn(123, "8.")  # put(123,8.) = "     123" #> [1] "     123"  # 8.2 rounds to two decimals. sas_f_putn(12.345, "8.2")  # put(12.345,8.2) = "   12.35" #> [1] "   12.35"  # Format 1. rounds 2.5 half away from zero: 3. sas_f_putn(2.5, "1.")  # put(2.5,1.) = "3" #> [1] "3"  # A value too wide for 8. is written in E notation. sas_f_putn(1e10, "8.")  # put(1e10,8.) = "    1E10" #> [1] "    1E10"  # DOLLAR10.2: dollar sign, thousands separator, minus sign. sas_f_putn(-1234.5, "dollar10.2")  # put(-1234.5,dollar10.2) = "$-1,234.50" #> [1] "$-1,234.50"  # PERCENT8.1 multiplies by 100 and adds a percent sign. sas_f_putn(0.125, "percent8.1")  # put(0.125,percent8.1) = "  12.5%" #> [1] "  12.5% "

title: SAS QUANTILE(distribution, probability <, parameters>) — sas_f_quantile
code: # QUANTILE: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # QUANTILE is approximate: in strict mode (the default) a direct call stops; these calls # run with options(sasonr.strict = FALSE) and a warning of class sasonr_strict_warning. old <- options(sasonr.strict = FALSE)  # For a discrete distribution the quantile is the smallest x with CDF >= p: the # binomial median is 5. sas_f_quantile("BINOMIAL", 0.5, 0.5, 10)  # quantile('BINOMIAL', 0.5, 0.5, 10) = 5 #> Warning: sasonr: function QUANTILE is approximate #> This warning is displayed once per session. #> [1] 5  # A missing probability gives a missing result. sas_f_quantile("NORMAL", NA_real_)  # quantile('NORMAL', .) = . #> [1] NA  options(old)

code: # QUOTE: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # QUOTE encloses the value in double quotation marks. sas_f_quote("abc")  # quote('abc') = "\"abc\"" #> [1] "\"abc\""  # An embedded double quotation mark is doubled. sas_f_quote("a\"b")  # quote('a"b') = "\"a\"\"b\"" #> [1] "\"a\"\"b\""  # The optional second argument chooses the quotation mark, here a single quote. sas_f_quote("abc", "'")  # quote('abc', "'") = "'abc'" #> [1] "'abc'"  # The literal '' is one blank, so the result is a blank enclosed in quotation # marks. sas_f_quote(" ")  # quote('') = "\" \"" #> [1] "\" \""

title: SAS ROUND(argument <, rounding-unit>) — sas_f_round
code: # ROUND: each call is explained above it and followed by its result # (dates are SAS day counts from 1960-01-01)  # Round to the nearest integer: halves go away from zero. sas_f_round(2.5)  # round(2.5) = 3 #> [1] 3  # Negative halves also go away from zero: -3. sas_f_round(-2.5)  # round(-2.5) = -3 #> [1] -3  # Rounding unit 0.1: ROUND treats 2.45 as the exact decimal, so 2.5 (base R # gives 2.4). sas_f_round(2.45, 0.1)  # round(2.45,0.1) = 2.5 #> [1] 2.5  # Rounding unit 0.01: 1.005 gives 1.01. sas_f_round(1.005, 0.01)  # round(1.005,0.01) = 1.01 #> [1] 1.01  # Rounding unit 100: the nearest multiple of 100. sas_f_round(1234.5678, 100)  # round(1234.5678,100) = 1200 #> [1] 1200  # A rounding unit of 1/3: the nearest multiple of 1/3. sas_f_round(2/3, 1/3)  # round(2/3,1/3) = 0.66666666666666 #> [1] 0.6666667

title: SAS ROUNDE(argument <, rounding-unit>) — sas_f_rounde
code: # ROUNDE: each call is explained above it and followed by its result  # ROUNDE rounds a value exactly halfway between two integers to the even one: # 2.5 gives 2. sas_f_rounde(2.5)  # rounde(2.5) = 2 #> [1] 2  # 3.5 is halfway between 3 and 4, so the even integer 4 is chosen. sas_f_rounde(3.5)  # rounde(3.5) = 4 #> [1] 4  # -2.5 is halfway between -3 and -2, so the even integer -2 is chosen. sas_f_rounde(-2.5)  # rounde(-2.5) = -2 #> [1] -2  # The second argument is the rounding unit: 2.45 is halfway between 2.4 and # 2.5, so the even multiple 2.4 is chosen. sas_f_rounde(2.45, 0.1)  # rounde(2.45, 0.1) = 2.4 #> [1] 2.4  # A missing argument gives a missing result. sas_f_rounde(NA_real_)  # rounde(.) = . #> [1] NA
